This is a lot of responsibility for an engineering manager to shoulder...

here's the problem with 2 week sprints for *many* teams

it is too long to learn how to work small (a big challenge for many teams)

it is too short to learn how to think big (a big challenge for many teams)

If you are forced to use the language of "to do" and "done" ... try this:

(Note: almost no one will get fired for doing this. You may get odd looks. But you owe it to your professional development to build this muscle.)

if you're being forced to provide a timeline-based roadmap ... do whatever you can to indicate the overarching mission/outcome.

just that visual hint can be a nudge

Fascinating what large enterprises have “on the list”

On the list:
————
Continuous discovery
OKRs
Story mapping
Impact mapping
Design sprints
Canvasses of various sorts
Scrum

Not on list:
————-
Shift from project to team funding
Direct access to customers

A large chunk of product management advice is targeted at 1) startups and/or 2) individual product management career advancement (eg “how can I get ahead”)

The problem. 1) most PMs don’t work at startups and 2) product is a team activity.
the jump from define big --> think big is challenging
Every company that has an innovation lab should also have a “boring shit that will actually save the business” lab.

Here’s how to make OKRs super easy

A. A strategy…a real one, which informs …

B. Some kind of persistent model, which inspires …

C.  Bets, experiments, whatever, and then …

D. Forecast the impact on that persistent model

A and B make C and D so much easier.
